blocks.text: A chessboard has 8 columns labeled a to h and 8 rows labeled 1 to 8. Every square is either black or white, and the colors alternate in both directions. Given a coordinate string like "c7", decide whether that square is white or black.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Checkerboard Kitchen Floor
blocks.text: Picture a kitchen floor tiled with alternating black and white tiles, starting with a black tile in the corner. If you want to know the color of a tile somewhere in the room, count how many tile-steps you would take from that corner, moving across and moving up. If the total number of steps is even, you land back on a black tile. If it is odd, you land on a white tile. A chessboard follows exactly this rule, with the a1 corner playing the role of that first black tile.

blocks.caption: The two rules a chessboard color follows

blocks.text: Before writing any code, it helps to reason through what a chessboard color actually depends on.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A chessboard's coloring is not random, it strictly alternates in both directions from one fixed anchor corner, a1, which is black.

Observation 2: Moving one step horizontally or vertically to a neighboring square always flips its color.

Observation 3: That means a square's color only depends on whether the total number of single steps away from the anchor corner is even or odd, not on the specific path taken to get there.

Observation 4: The total number of steps away from a1, in board terms, is exactly the column index plus the row index. The entire board's coloring collapses into one parity check, no simulation needed.
That reasoning alone already points straight at the optimized solution: no grid needs to exist, only a column index, a row index, and a parity check.

The most literal way to solve this is to actually build the chessboard: an 8 by 8 grid, filled one cell at a time with alternating colors, starting from a black corner. Once the grid exists, answering the question is just a single lookup at the given row and column.

items: Create an empty 8 by 8 grid.
Fill every cell: a cell is black when its row index plus column index is even, white otherwise.
Convert the input coordinate (like "c7") into a row index and a column index.
Return whatever color is stored at that row and column in the grid.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: build the whole board, then look up one cell

codes.python:
def square_is_white(coordinates):
    # build an 8 by 8 board, alternating colors like a real chessboard
    board = []
    for r in range(8):
        row_colors = []
        for c in range(8):
            # r=0, c=0 (the a1 corner) is black on a real board
            row_colors.append("black" if (r + c) % 2 == 0 else "white")
        board.append(row_colors)
    # convert the coordinate string, for example "c7", into board indices
    col = ord(coordinates[0]) - ord('a')   # 'a' to 'h' becomes 0 to 7
    row = int(coordinates[1]) - 1          # '1' to '8' becomes 0 to 7
    # look the color up in the board we just built
    return board[row][col] == "white"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    coordinates = "h3"
    print(square_is_white(coordinates))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The board is filled using (r + c) % 2 == 0 for black specifically because that is the exact rule a real chessboard follows anchored at a1, so the simulation has to match reality before it can be trusted as a lookup table.
The coordinate is parsed with simple character arithmetic rather than any parsing library, since the input is guaranteed to always be exactly one letter followed by one digit.

Building the entire 8 by 8 board before answering a single query is intentionally wasteful here, it exists specifically to set up the contrast with the optimized version, not because it is a good solution on its own.

blocks.text: This works because the grid is filled using the exact same alternating rule a real chessboard follows, anchored at a black a1 corner. Every cell ends up the correct color before it is ever read.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1). The board is always exactly 8 by 8, so filling it is always 64 fixed steps, regardless of the input.
Space: O(1) as well, but with a much bigger constant, since a whole 64 cell grid is allocated just to answer a single query.

Limitation: this problem does not have an input that grows, the board size is always fixed at 8 by 8. So the brute force is not slow in the traditional sense, its real weakness is wasted work: building 64 cells of a grid just to read one of them, when the color of a single square can be worked out directly from its coordinate.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why simulate the whole board at all: building 64 cells just to answer one query does far more work than the question actually requires.

What it wastes: 62 of the 64 cells filled are thrown away unused, only one of them is ever read.

Can we skip the grid entirely: yes, since every cell's color already comes from one simple rule, row plus column parity, applied identically to every cell.

Do we need to build anything just to apply that rule once: no, the same parity check can be applied directly to the one coordinate being asked about.

The core idea: convert the coordinate straight into column and row indices, add them, and check even or odd. No grid, no wasted cells.

The grid never actually needs to exist. The color of any square is fully determined by a simple pattern: whether the column index plus the row index is even or odd. That is exactly the same rule the brute force uses to fill each cell, so there is no reason to fill 64 cells just to reuse that rule once.
The optimization is to apply the rule directly to the one coordinate that was asked about, and skip building any grid at all.
Convert the column letter and row number into zero based indices, add them together, and check whether the sum is even or odd. An even sum means black, an odd sum means white.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Check","Value","Why"],"rows":[["1","col = d minus a","3","Converts the column letter into a zero based index."],["2","row = 4 minus 1","3","Converts the 1 indexed row digit into a zero based index."],["3","sum = col + row","6","Combines both indices into the single value the parity rule cares about."],["4","sum is even","Black","An even sum always matches the color of the black a1 anchor corner."]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: compute the parity directly, no grid

codes.python:
def square_is_white(coordinates):
    col = ord(coordinates[0]) - ord('a')   # 'a' to 'h' becomes 0 to 7, no grid needed
    row = int(coordinates[1]) - 1          # '1' to '8' becomes 0 to 7
    # an even sum lands on a black square, an odd sum lands on a white square
    return (col + row) % 2 != 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    coordinates = "h3"
    print(square_is_white(coordinates))

blocks.text: This works because the parity of column plus row is mathematically identical to the color the brute force grid would have stored at that exact cell, since both use the exact same rule. Skipping the grid does not change the rule, it just avoids computing it 63 extra times for cells nobody asked about.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What It Means","Result"],"rows":[["col + row is even","The coordinate is an even number of total steps away from the black a1 anchor corner","Black"],["col + row is odd","The coordinate is an odd number of total steps away from the black a1 anchor corner, so the color has flipped","White"]]}

items: col and row are computed with simple character subtraction against a and 1, rather than any lookup, because ASCII values are already contiguous and ordered for both letters and digits.
The parity check uses modulo 2 on the sum of col and row, not on either one separately, since it is the combined step count away from the anchor that determines color.
Returning (col + row) % 2 != 0 directly as the boolean, instead of an if/else, keeps the function to one line since the parity check already is the answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), just two subtractions, one addition, and one modulo check.
Space: O(1), a couple of integers, no grid allocated at all.

The optimized solution is already doing the minimum possible work: read 2 characters, do a constant number of arithmetic operations, return 1 boolean. There is no asymptotic improvement left to make, both time and space are already O(1) with a tiny constant.

A common interview variation worth knowing anyway: checking parity with addition and modulo can be replaced with XOR and a bitmask, since XOR-ing the last bit of two numbers gives the same even or odd answer as adding them and checking modulo 2. This is not faster in any measurable way for a problem this small, it is purely a bitwise style some interviewers like to see recognized.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action","Value","Why"],"rows":[["1","col = c minus a","2","Same column conversion as the optimized version."],["2","row = 7 minus 1","6","Same row conversion as the optimized version."],["3","col XOR row (binary 010 XOR 110)","4 (binary 100)","XOR-ing the two indices bit by bit is set up to mirror addition mod 2 on their lowest bit."],["4","(col XOR row) AND 1","0, so the square is Black","Masking with 1 isolates just the lowest bit, which is all that parity ever depended on."]]}

codes.python:
def square_is_white(coordinates):
    col = ord(coordinates[0]) - ord('a')
    row = int(coordinates[1]) - 1
    # XOR of the last bits is equivalent to checking (col + row) % 2,
    # a common interview micro-variant, not a complexity improvement
    return ((col ^ row) & 1) == 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    coordinates = "h3"
    print(square_is_white(coordinates))

items: XOR-ing col and row directly mirrors addition-then-modulo-2 specifically because XOR of the lowest bit of two numbers produces exactly the same 0 or 1 result as (col + row) % 2, a well known bit identity, not a coincidence.
Masking with & 1 after the XOR isolates just the lowest bit, since XOR of two numbers can be larger than 1 in its higher bits, only the lowest bit ever matters for parity.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), identical to the optimized solution.
Space: O(1), identical to the optimized solution. This variant is a style choice, not a complexity win.

blocks.text: The core pattern here is recognizing a fixed, well known alternating structure (a chessboard) and expressing its rule as direct arithmetic instead of simulating the structure itself. Not every optimization changes the complexity class, sometimes the real win is removing wasted constant-factor work, exactly like this problem's jump from building 64 cells down to 2 subtractions.

items: Mixing up which corner is black. On a standard board, a1 is black, this anchors the whole parity rule.
Off by one errors converting the row character, remember the row digit is 1 indexed in the input but needs to become 0 indexed for the parity check.
Assuming a bigger board means this needs to scale, when the board size is always fixed at 8 by 8 regardless of input.

blocks.text: This is a good problem for showing you can spot when a problem is really just disguised parity math. Starting with the honest brute force (build the board) and then explaining why it is unnecessary, rather than jumping straight to the formula, demonstrates the reasoning interviewers actually want to see.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid building the board", think: direct parity check on the two indices.
If the interviewer says "can you do this without modulo", think: XOR the two indices and mask the lowest bit.
If the interviewer says "what if the board were n by n", think: the same parity rule still holds, since it never depended on the board being exactly 8 by 8 to begin with.

items: Can you solve this without building the full board?
Can you do the parity check without the modulo operator?
What changes if the board were n by n instead of a fixed 8 by 8?
What if the anchor corner, a1, were white instead of black, how would the rule change?
Can you generalize this to any two color alternating grid, not just a chessboard?
Any problem describing a fixed, regularly alternating structure (checkerboards, striped patterns, alternating rows) where the real question is disguised parity math.
Grid coloring and graph 2-coloring problems, where reachability between cells in an even or odd number of steps determines which of two groups a cell belongs to.
Bit manipulation problems that swap a modulo-2 check for an XOR and bitmask, the exact same identity used in this problem's further optimization.
Coordinate-to-index conversion patterns (letter-to-number, 1-indexed-to-0-indexed) that show up constantly in spreadsheet, chessboard, and grid based problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Every approach here runs in O(1) time and O(1) space, since the board size never grows. The meaningful difference between them is the size of the constant factor: 64 units of wasted work in the brute force, versus a small handful of arithmetic operations in the optimized and bitwise versions.

items: Pattern: disguised parity math over a fixed size alternating grid, not a real simulation problem.
Core Idea: a cell's color only depends on whether its column index plus row index is even or odd, relative to a fixed black anchor corner (a1); no grid ever needs to be built.
Time: O(1) across every version shown here.
Space: O(1) across every version; only the brute force wastes space building an unused 8x8 grid.

Most Important Observation: this problem's brute force is not slow, it is wasteful, since the board size never grows; the win is removing constant-factor waste, not improving an asymptotic complexity class.
Interview Difficulty: easy on the surface, but recognizing "this is just parity math, not board simulation" is exactly what separates a strong answer from a mechanical one.
One line memory trick: do not build the board, just add the two indices and check even or odd.
